prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network scored 0 because it learned to press DONE at once. The likely cause is the hidden rule. Target, missing, extra and target-height channels are shifted 4 columns, which is half the 8-wide grid. The starting network only combines nearby cells: its two 3x3 convolutions see a 5x5 area. So when it scores a placement at column x, it cannot see the missing cells, which sit at column x+4. Random placements mostly fill wrong cells and lose reward, while DONE costs nothing, so the policy collapses to DONE. Every candidate therefore needs a learned layer whose reach covers the whole row, so it can find the shift itself; I do not hard-code a roll by 4. Candidate 1 adds a full-width, wrap-around convolution on the target channels with the default recipe. Candidate 2 is the same network with more updates and more entropy to resist the DONE collapse. Candidate 3 uses attention over all cells, with a learned bias for each relative position.

### Round 2
r1c1 is the only trial that learned (0.139: 0.150 and 0.127). Wrap-around full-row/column convolutions on the target stream can undo the 4-column roll. The starting net, r1c2 and r1c3 all collapsed to DONE at step 1. r1c2 used r1c1's network with a different recipe, so the collapse comes from training dynamics too. Early random placements earn negative reward and DONE earns 0. Even r1c1 dropped to 2.9 steps per episode at 25% of training before recovering. r1c1 also looks undertrained: training success rose from 0.034 to 0.105 in the last quarter. It fails by stopping early on upper layers and overhangs (IoU 0.76, almost no cells outside the target). This round is a 2x2 test against r1c1: (a) a DONE logit measured relative to the placement logits, so pushing all placements down no longer makes DONE win; (b) a cheaper x-only realignment with early fusion, giving about 25% more samples; (c) both.

### Round 3
The shifted target was the main obstacle. Every network without an explicit wrap-around realignment collapsed to calling DONE first. Learned full-row wrap-around convolutions fixed that, and the cheaper early-fusion version r2c2 is the best so far at 0.43. Its two seeds scored 0.31 and 0.54, so seed noise is about ±0.12. The relative DONE logit did not help: r2c3 scored 0.25 against r2c2's 0.43. r2c2's training success was still rising at the end of the budget, so more samples may help. Training takes about 60 s, so time is not a constraint. The traces show two failures. The agent calls DONE while cells are still missing, and it misses high placements over gaps (for example a 1x2 brick resting at layer 2 on one supporting column). Fixing these needs a stronger incentive to finish and a head that knows which cell under the brick supports it. r1c2's collapse mixed several changes at once (n_envs 128, entropy 0.02, a heavier network), so it does not show that 2 PPO epochs fail.

### Round 4
Realigning the shifted target with a learned wrap-around full-row convolution is what made learning possible (the starting net and the transformer both stayed at 0). The cheap early-fusion version, r2c2, is best at 0.43 (0.31 and 0.54). r3c1 uses the same net with 2 PPO epochs and scored about the same mean (0.42), but one seed reached 0.77 and the other only 0.08. More samples can therefore help a lot, but early learning is unreliable. Three changes did not help, within seed noise: the relative DONE logit, a longer horizon (gamma 0.99, which clearly hurt) and the footprint-convolution head. Higher entropy (0.02) went with a full collapse to DONE in both round-1 trials that used it. The failures look like slow or unlucky discovery of the shift early in training. So this round tests a shared shift kernel that should make alignment faster and more reliable, plus a middle ground of 3 PPO epochs.

## Trial it ended with
name: Shared shift kernel, 2 epochs
hypothesis: Combines the shared shift kernel (candidate 1) with 2 PPO epochs. In r3c1, 2 epochs reached 0.77 on one seed but failed on the other, which looks like a slow, seed-dependent discovery of the shift. If a shared 8-weight shift makes alignment fast and reliable, both seeds should get the benefit of about 1.9x the samples. Refuted if mean dev success is not above 0.43, or if one seed again stays below 0.15.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: The rule is stated in Round 1: "Target, missing, extra and target-height channels are shifted 4 columns, which is half the 8-wide grid... the missing cells, which sit at column x+4." Round 2 then calls it "the 4-column roll" that wrap-around convolutions can undo. Together these give what is changed (the four target channels), the amount (4 columns), the direction (toward higher x) and the wrap-around.
